summary: A 28-second Doritos spot built as a single continuous visual gag: a grandmother teases a baby with chips, a sound-design hinge-cord shot foreshadows a slingshot rig, speech drops to near-silence as tension builds, and a one-line punchline ('Excuse me') lands in the final seconds. The ad relies almost entirely on b-roll/visual comedy and a wide dynamic audio range rather than dialogue density or on-screen branding.

structure.label: Grandma asks 'Who has the Doritos?' while baby watches
Teasing exchange, chips withheld from baby
Silent build-up, no dialogue, rising loudness

hook.what_happens: An elderly woman in a wheelchair-like chair sits beside a baby in a jumper/swing in a backyard, asking twice 'Who has the Doritos?' before teasing the baby with 'You want one? Sorry.'
hook.promise: A comedic payoff involving the chips and the baby's swing rig
strengths: Opens on spoken words at 0.0s with a direct question, giving an immediate narrative hook (questions_per_min 6.34, 75th pct in category)
Fast early cutting (hook_cuts 10, 75th pct) keeps the odd juxtaposition of grandmother and baby visually active
Unusual visual pairing (wheelchair, swing, backyard) creates curiosity before any punchline is revealed
weaknesses: No on-screen text or branding appears in the first 3 seconds (hook_text_overlay false, 42nd pct), so viewers scrolling without sound get no brand cue
Opening visual (wide static backyard shot) is low-motion and ambiguous about what the gag will be, relying entirely on dialogue to signal intent

strengths.point: The ad builds tension through an extended quiet stretch and rising loudness/energy before the reveal, a classic ad-comedy timing device
The spot leans fully on visual storytelling and face-forward b-roll rather than talking-head exposition, matching a cinematic Super Bowl ad style

evidence.value: An old woman in a wheelchair sitting next to a baby in a jumper in a backyard.

strengths.point: A close-up insert of a bungee/spring cord mid-sequence quietly foreshadows the physical gag without dialogue, letting the visual carry plot information

evidence.value: Close-up of a stretched bungee/spring cord against a porch backdrop

recommendations.title: Add branding/text to reinforce sound-off viewing
recommendations.observation: The spot has zero on-screen text across its entire runtime, well below typical category levels
recommendations.recommendation: Test adding a small logo or product text in the first 3 seconds so sound-off or distracted viewers can still identify the brand before the punchline lands

recommendations.title: Consider a closing CTA/brand card
recommendations.observation: cta_count is 0, well below the ad category's typical 1-2 calls to action, and there is no first_cta_pos recorded
recommendations.recommendation: Test appending a brief end card with the product name/tagline after the punchline so the payoff still lands narratively while leaving a clear brand touchpoint

recommendations.title: Examine the 15-25s dialogue lull before the payoff
recommendations.observation: Words-per-minute drops to 12 then 0 in consecutive bins right before the final punchline, the longest stretch of the ad without speech
recommendations.recommendation: If this silence is meant to build suspense, consider testing whether a sound effect or visual cue mid-pause keeps engagement before the 'Excuse me' line, since the pause is unusually long relative to the category's long_pauses_per_min benchmark

recommendations.title: Shot-length variability is unusually uniform
recommendations.observation: Shot-length CV of 0.32 sits at the 8th percentile for ads, meaning cuts are far more evenly timed than most ads in the corpus, which typically vary shot length more for comedic emphasis
recommendations.recommendation: Test varying shot duration more around the punchline (e.g., a longer hold before 'Excuse me' and a quicker cut after) to see if it sharpens comedic timing
